newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says China silenced dissent.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says China silenced dissent.

text.p: The United States on Thursday accused China of effectively silencing all public dissent against the communist party and government in 1996.

In its 20th annual human rights report of 193 countries, the State Department also faulted the records of allies Turkey, South Korea and Germany plus Russia, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Burma and U.S. "terrorist list" states: Cuba, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Sudan, Syria and North Korea.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said human rights would remain a "key element" in U.S. foreign policy.

"When human rights standards are observed, sustainable economic progress is more likely, violent conflicts are easier to prevent, terrorists and criminals find it harder to operate," she told reporters in marking release of the report.

She also told reporters she had a particular concern about religious persecution, saying: "In too many countries from Sudan, to Vietnam to Iran, this form of repression persists. In a few including China, it has increased."

The department's findings on China were of keen interest because of U.S. efforts to build a better relationship with the communist giant, and the conclusion was that "no dissidents were known to be active (in China) at year's end."

China "in 1996 continued to commit widespread and well-documented human rights abuses, in violation of internationally-accepted norms, stemming from the authorities' intolerance of dissent, fear of unrest and the continuing absence of laws protecting basic freedoms," it said.
"All public dissent against party and government was effectively silenced by intimidation, exile or the imposition of prison terms, administrative detention or house arrest."
Washington regularly criticises Beijing's record in its annual human rights assessment. But this year's report comes as the two were striving to improve ties.
The report's conclusion would seem to make it impossible for Washington not to sponsor a controversial resolution at the Human Rights Commission in Geneva faulting China's record.
U.S. officials told Reuters they expect the United States to proceed with the resolution in conjunction with European allies even though it is unlikely to be adopted.

Albright has said she will pursue a policy of integration rather than isolation towards China and, while keen to foster human rights, will make ties conditional on any one issue. She will visit Beijing next month on her first overseas trip.

The report said Turkey had "serious human rights problems" in 1996 and its record deteriorated in some respects. "The (Turkish) government was unable to sustain improvements made in 1995 and, as a result, its record was uneven in 1996 and deteriorated in some respects," it said.

The section on South Korea said violence against women, especially rape, is a serious problem there. "Women continued to face legal and societal discrimination. Violence against women and physical abuse remain serious problems," it said.
The department took issue with Germany for discriminating against Scientology in business and cultural life, but cited "some positive developments" in Bonn's treatment of the group.
Washington's alliance with Saudi Arabia did not prevent sharp criticism of the kingdom government, which the report said "commits and tolerates serious human rights abuses".
The Afghanistan review said "discrimination (against women) reached new heights of severity ... with the rise to power of the Taliban," the Moslems ruling much of that land.
The report said Russia's rights record showed little progress last year, with Russians using "indiscriminate and disproportionate" force in the breakaway Republic of Chechnya.

It found Indonesia continued to commit serious human rights abuses in 1996, including in East Timor. "While Indonesia exhibits a surface adherence to democractic firms, its political system remains strongly authoritarian," it said.
Political killings in Haiti rose from 1995, but remained far fewer than before the U.S. military operation that restored the first democratically elected president, it said.
In the Middle East, it said Israel's withdrawal from the West Bank led to improved human rights but both Israel and the Palestinian Authority continue to commit serious abuses.
Human rights in communist-ruled Cuba worsened last year with a crackdown on a pro-democracy umbrella group and many other alleged abuses of power, the report said.
Nigeria's human rights performance was called dismal, while Burma's military regime was faulted for continued repression of its democratic political opposition.
